summary: Zayd ibn Harithah (RA) was the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and the first man outside the immediate family to accept Islam. His unique relationship with the Prophet ﷺ — of deep paternal affection that was acknowledged publicly and affirmed in revelation — makes him one of the most personally significant Companions. He was martyred at the Battle of Mu'tah in 8 AH and is the only Companion mentioned by name in the Quran.
biography:
Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi was born around 581 CE into the Banu Kalb tribe of Arabia. As a child he was taken captive during a tribal raid, brought to Makkah, and sold in the slave market, where he was purchased by Khadijah bint Khuwaylid (RA). When the Prophet ﷺ married Khadijah, she gave Zayd to him as a gift. The Prophet ﷺ, recognizing the boy's qualities, treated him not as a slave but as a beloved son.

When Zayd's father Harithah and uncle Ka'b discovered where Zayd was, they came to Makkah prepared to ransom him. The Prophet ﷺ gave Zayd the choice: return with his father and uncle, or remain with him. Zayd chose to remain with the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ was so moved that he took Zayd to the Kaaba, in front of all the Quraysh, and publicly declared him his son. Thereafter Zayd was known as Zayd ibn Muhammad — son of Muhammad — and was given full social standing as an adopted son. This practice of adoption with name transfer was common in pre-Islamic Arabia. Ibn Sa'd records this account in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra.

Zayd was among the first people to accept Islam — the first free adult male or among the very first after Khadijah (RA) and Ali ibn Abi Talib (RA). He was also among the first to pray behind the Prophet ﷺ. His early faith earned him the title Hibb Rasul Allah — the Beloved of the Messenger of Allah — used by the Companions to describe the deep affection the Prophet ﷺ held for him.

A pivotal moment in Islamic law occurred in connection with Zayd's marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh (RA), a woman of noble Qurayshi lineage. When that marriage ended in divorce and the Prophet ﷺ subsequently married Zaynab, the Quraysh and some in the Muslim community used it to criticize the Prophet ﷺ for marrying his son's ex-wife. Allah revealed verses addressing this directly (Quran 33:37-40), clarifying that Zayd was the Prophet's ﷺ adopted, not biological, son, and that the pre-Islamic practice of treating adopted sons as biological sons in all legal respects was abolished. The verses explicitly named Zayd: 'So when Zayd had dissolved from her all obligation in divorce...' (Quran 33:37). This makes Zayd the only Companion explicitly named in the Quran. The revelation also abolished the prohibition on marrying the ex-wives of adopted sons, distinguishing adoption from biological paternity in Islamic law.

Zayd served as a military commander on multiple occasions, a mark of the Prophet's ﷺ trust in his ability. He led the expedition to al-Qardah (5 AH), the expedition to Umm Qirfah (6 AH), and several other operations. The Prophet ﷺ trusted him with command over some of his most senior Companions.

In 8 AH (629 CE), the Prophet ﷺ sent an expedition to Mu'tah in present-day Jordan, one of the first Muslim encounters with Byzantine-allied forces. He appointed Zayd as its commander, with Jafar ibn Abi Talib (RA) as his deputy and Abd Allah ibn Rawahah (RA) as third in command. When the Muslim force encountered a massive Byzantine and allied Arab army at Mu'tah, Zayd fought carrying the Prophet's ﷺ banner and was killed in the engagement. Jafar then took the banner, lost both arms in combat, carried it with his chest until he too was killed. The Prophet ﷺ learned of the battle through revelation while sitting in Madinah before the messengers arrived, and he announced the deaths to the Companions with tears in his eyes. He described seeing Zayd, Jafar, and Ibn Rawahah in Paradise: 'They were raised in the presence of the throne, faces illuminated.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Maghazi).

Zayd's son Usamah ibn Zayd (RA) went on to become one of the most beloved young Companions of the Prophet ﷺ and was appointed commander of an army by the Prophet ﷺ shortly before his death — an army that included Abu Bakr and Umar (RA) as soldiers. Zayd is buried at Mu'tah, where his tomb is visited to this day.
